# How to Read Through Insurance Policies and Bank Contracts with Claude

> **In short:** Paste any insurance policy, loan agreement, or bank contract into Claude and ask for a plain-English summary. Claude will flag hidden fees, exclusions, and tricky clauses — but it cannot replace a lawyer, and very long documents may need to be split into parts.

Insurance policies and bank contracts are written in a style called *legalese* — language that sounds official but is designed to be hard to read. A 30-page home insurance PDF often hides the answer to "am I actually covered if my pipe bursts?" in paragraph 47. Claude can read that whole document in seconds and explain it like a friend would over coffee. Here's how to use it without losing the details that matter.

## Before you start
- A free Claude account at **claude.com** (the free plan is enough for short documents; very long contracts may need a paid plan with a bigger file upload).
- The contract or policy you want to read — either as a PDF file on your device, or as text you can copy from your email.
- About 10–15 minutes for your first try.
- A quiet moment. You'll want to actually read Claude's summary, not just skim it.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh chat with Claude
Go to **claude.com** and log in. Click **"New chat"** at the top-left of the screen. A blank conversation box opens. Starting fresh matters because Claude remembers the previous conversation — and you don't want yesterday's homework question mixed up with today's insurance policy. If you're on the phone app, tap the **pencil or "New chat" icon** instead; if you can't find it, look for a button like **"Start new conversation"**.
💬 Example: there is nothing to type yet — just open the chat.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box with a **paperclip icon** (for attaching files) and a **send arrow**.

## Step 2 — Attach the document (or paste the text)
Click the **paperclip icon** 📎 to the left of the message box, then choose your file (PDF, Word, or a photo of a printed page usually works). If your contract is already open in another window, you can also simply copy the text — **Ctrl+C** on Windows or **⌘+C** on Mac — and paste it straight into the chat box with **Ctrl+V** or **⌘+V**. After you attach or paste, you'll see a small file thumbnail or a chunk of text appear in the box. If you don't see a paperclip, look for a **"+" button** or an **upload icon** instead — apps change the icon from time to time.
💬 Example: a PDF named `home-insurance-2026.pdf` shows up as a thumbnail before you send.
You'll know it worked when Claude replies that it has read the document and is ready for your question.

## Step 3 — Ask for a plain-English summary first
Before asking tricky questions, ask Claude to give you the basics. A good first prompt tells Claude who you are and what kind of document it is. Type a short message in the box, then press **Enter** or tap the **send arrow**. Claude will write a multi-paragraph reply covering the main points. If the reply is too short or too long, follow up with "Can you go deeper on the parts a normal person would care about?"
💬 Example: "I'm a homeowner, not a lawyer. Please summarize this home insurance policy in plain English. Cover: what am I covered for, what am I NOT covered for, my deductible, and anything that could void my coverage. Keep it under 400 words."
You'll know it worked when Claude's reply lists the key sections in everyday language, with no big unexplained words.

## Step 4 — Ask Claude to flag the "gotcha" clauses
Now for the part that saves real money. Many contracts include clauses (sentences or whole sections) that limit what the company has to pay you — things like "we only cover damage from sudden events, not gradual wear." Type a follow-up question in the same chat. Claude uses what it already read, so you don't need to re-upload anything. If the reply feels vague, add "Give me at least five specific examples."
💬 Example: "Now read it again like a skeptical friend. List every clause that could limit my payout or surprise me. For each one, quote the original wording, then explain what it actually means in plain English."
You'll know it worked when Claude gives you a bulleted list with both the original sentence and a plain translation — those are the spots to read twice in the real document.

## Step 5 — Compare two offers side by side (optional but powerful)
If you're choosing between two insurance quotes or loan offers, open a second chat (back to **"New chat"**) and upload both documents — or paste both into the same chat one after the other. Then ask Claude to compare them on the points that matter to you. Claude reads both files in seconds and builds a comparison. Be specific about what you want to compare, because "which is better?" is too vague to answer well.
💬 Example: "I've pasted two home loan offers below. Compare them on: total interest paid over 5 years, early-repayment penalties, fixed vs variable rate, and any hidden fees. Show your work in a simple table."
You'll know it worked when Claude produces a clean table or side-by-side list — and you can spot the better deal in about a minute.

## Step 6 — Save the summary where you'll actually find it
Claude's replies disappear if you lose the browser tab. Before you close the chat, copy the most useful reply (the summary, the gotcha list, or the comparison) into a notes app, email it to yourself, or take a screenshot. On a computer, click and drag to highlight the reply, then **Ctrl+C / ⌘+C**. On a phone, long-press the text and choose **"Copy"** or **"Share"**. Saving this now means you don't have to ask Claude again six months later when you actually need the info.
💬 Example: paste into a note titled `home-insurance-summary-2026` so future-you can find it.
You'll know it worked when you can close Claude, reopen your notes app, and see the summary waiting for you.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting only the first page.** Insurance policies often hide the most important exclusions near the end. If the file is long, upload the whole PDF instead of copying a paragraph.
- **Trusting the summary without checking the originals.** Claude is helpful, but it can occasionally miss a clause or misread a number. Always open the real document and confirm any decision that affects money or coverage.
- **Asking vague questions like "is this a good deal?"** Claude needs specifics to compare well. Name the criteria (fees, interest rate, coverage limits, cancellation terms) so the answer is useful.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Reading a car insurance renewal no longer means an hour of squinting. Ten minutes with Claude gets you the parts that matter before you sign.
- **For your business or work:** Comparing supplier contracts or client terms of service becomes a 15-minute task instead of an afternoon — useful for freelancers and small-business owners who don't have legal staff on call.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one document you've been meaning to read — a bank fee schedule, a phone plan, an old insurance renewal — and run it through Steps 2 and 3 today. The habit starts there.

## Try it now
Find one PDF or email attachment from your bank, insurer, or phone company that you've been avoiding. Open a new Claude chat, upload it, and paste this prompt: *"I'm not a lawyer. Summarize this in plain English, then list the three things in here that could cost me money if I don't know about them."* Read the reply once, then decide whether the document deserves a closer look — that one minute of friction-free reading is the whole point.
